blocks.text:
Design the real-time video and audio conferencing system behind something like Zoom, where several people join the same call, see and hear each other live, and the whole experience keeps working reasonably well even when someone's home internet connection is having a bad day. This problem is a genuine departure from everything else in this category. WhatsApp, Slack, and even the live comment stream on a video are all fundamentally about moving discrete pieces of data, a message or a comment, from one place to another reliably. A video call is about moving a continuous stream of audio and video samples with almost no tolerance for delay, and a surprisingly high tolerance for occasionally losing a piece of it entirely.

The single idea that shapes almost every decision in this design is that a video call has two completely separate jobs: figuring out who is talking to whom and how (signaling), and actually moving the audio and video bits between them fast (media transport). Keeping those two jobs on two entirely different paths, rather than treating a video call like one more kind of message to route, is what makes the rest of this design make sense.

blocks.text: Users need to be able to create and join a meeting, with multiple participants sending and receiving audio and video simultaneously. A participant should be able to share their screen instead of, or alongside, their camera. Meetings should support muting your own audio or video, and a host should be able to mute others. The active speaker, whoever is currently talking, should be visually highlighted for everyone. A meeting should optionally be recorded and made available afterward. A large meeting should support a webinar mode, one or a few presenters broadcasting to a large, mostly silent audience.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and a couple of them are close to the opposite of what mattered in the text-based systems earlier in this category.

blocks.alt: Ultra-low latency, loss tolerance, adaptiveness to bandwidth, scalability to large meetings, and secure media transport

blocks.text: Latency has to stay under roughly a hundred and fifty milliseconds one way or a conversation starts to feel unnatural, people talk over each other because they cannot tell if the other side has actually finished speaking. Loss tolerance is the sharpest reversal compared to a chat message: a dropped video frame is simply skipped and the next one is shown, retransmitting it would arrive too late to be useful anyway, so this system happily trades perfect delivery for staying current. Adaptiveness matters because real networks fluctuate constantly, and a participant's quality should degrade smoothly rather than freeze entirely when their bandwidth drops. Scalability has an unusually wide range here, an ordinary call has a handful of people, but a webinar can have thousands of silent viewers watching one presenter, and those are almost different problems architecturally. And media has to be encrypted in transit the whole way, since a video call is about as sensitive a data stream as a platform carries.

blocks.text: This design uses a Selective Forwarding Unit architecture rather than a full mesh or a Multipoint Control Unit, for reasons worked through in detail in section 24. Media travels over UDP using RTP, encrypted as SRTP, since UDP's willingness to drop rather than retransmit is exactly what low-latency media transport wants. A TURN relay is assumed as a fallback path for participants behind especially restrictive NATs or firewalls, where a direct connection to the SFU cannot be established. Recording, when enabled, captures server-side at the SFU rather than stitching together each participant's local recording. Phone dial-in is treated as a gateway that translates a phone call into the same RTP stream everything else uses, not a fundamentally different path.

blocks.text: At peak, the platform might be handling a million concurrent calls. The overwhelming majority of those are small, four to six participants, which is the shape this design optimizes for by default. The outlier case, a large webinar with one or a few presenters and up to ten thousand viewers, is architecturally different enough that it gets its own topology in section 17 rather than being treated as just a bigger version of an ordinary call. Bandwidth-wise, a single participant sending HD video costs roughly one and a half megabits per second, and that number, multiplied across every participant in a call and then across every simultaneous call on the platform, is what actually drives infrastructure cost, examined further in section 25.

blocks.text: Two paths run in parallel and almost never talk to each other directly. The signaling path is a fairly ordinary WebSocket-based service: it tells a joining client which SFU instance is hosting their meeting, and relays the SDP offers, answers, and ICE candidates each client needs to establish its actual media connection. Once that handshake finishes, the signaling server steps out of the way entirely, and every subsequent audio and video packet flows directly between the client and the SFU, never through the signaling server at all. The SFU is the one place actually doing work on the media itself: each participant uploads their audio and video exactly once, and the SFU selectively forwards those streams to whichever other participants need them, at whatever quality level fits each recipient's bandwidth.

blocks.text: This is the single most important architectural fork in the whole problem, and it is worth seeing all three options side by side before committing to one.
blocks.content: This is the single most important architectural fork in the whole problem, and it is worth seeing all three options side by side before committing to one.

blocks.alt: A full mesh has every client connect to every other client directly and its upload cost grows with each new participant; an SFU has every client upload once while the server selectively forwards; an MCU has the server decode and mix every stream into one combined stream

blocks.text: A full mesh is the simplest option conceptually and needs no media server at all, but a client's upload cost grows with every additional participant, since it has to send its own stream separately to each one, which makes it fall apart past a handful of people. An MCU keeps client bandwidth low no matter how large the call gets, since the server does all the mixing, but that mixing means the server has to decode and re-encode every single stream, a heavy, expensive compute cost per call. The SFU sits in between: a client uploads exactly once regardless of how many people are in the call, and the server does comparatively cheap work, forwarding packets rather than decoding and re-encoding them, which is why it is the right default for the participant counts this system actually needs to support.

blocks.text: An SFU's forwarding decision is not all-or-nothing. Each client actually uploads several quality versions of its own video at once, called simulcast layers, and the SFU picks which layer to forward to each individual recipient based on that recipient's own available bandwidth.

blocks.text: This schema is intentionally small, because almost nothing about a live call is durable data in the traditional sense. The one field worth calling out is assignedSfuId on Meeting, which is exactly what lets the signaling server tell a joining participant which SFU instance to connect to, and what makes SFU failover in section 20 possible to coordinate.

blocks.text: Almost all of the interesting state during a call, who is currently speaking, who is subscribed to which simulcast layer, current packet loss per participant, lives in the SFU's own memory for the duration of the call and is never written to a database at all. The only durable records are meeting scheduling metadata, the participant roster, and, if recording was enabled, a pointer to where the recorded file ended up in object storage. This is a deliberately thin persistence layer, because trying to durably persist every moment of a live call's ephemeral state would add latency to the one path in this whole system that can least afford it.

A participant whose network is degrading is switched by the SFU from a high simulcast layer to a low one, trading quality for continuity instead of freezing

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the join flow above: a client connects, negotiates, and starts sending and receiving media within a couple of round trips. The workflow worth walking through separately is what happens when a direct connection cannot be established at all, which happens more often than it might seem, since plenty of home and corporate networks sit behind NATs or firewalls that block unsolicited inbound connections. The client and the SFU first try to connect directly using addresses learned from a STUN server. If that fails, both sides fall back to relaying every packet through a TURN server instead, which works reliably but costs an extra network hop and doubles the bandwidth that hop consumes, since the TURN server has to both receive and re-send everything.

Live audio and video is never cached, since it exists only for the instant it is shown; meeting metadata and the participant list cache normally, since they barely change during a call

blocks.text: It is worth being explicit about what caching does not apply to here, since that is a genuinely different answer than almost every other system in this document. There is no sense in which a video frame from three seconds ago is worth caching, it is simply gone. The only things worth caching at all are the boring, low-volume pieces: who is in the meeting, what the meeting's title is, whether recording is currently enabled.

blocks.alt: The SFU forwards a copy of the media asynchronously to a recording queue, which an encoder consumes and writes to durable storage, entirely decoupled from the live call

blocks.text: Recording is the one place in this design that genuinely benefits from an async queue, precisely because it is the one output that does not need to happen in real time at all, the recording only needs to exist sometime after the meeting ends, which frees it to run behind a queue without ever touching the latency-sensitive live path.

blocks.alt: A participant joining an existing meeting is routed to whichever SFU instance is already hosting it; a brand-new meeting is assigned to the nearest healthy SFU instance

blocks.text: Like the document router in a collaborative editor, this is sticky rather than round robin, but for a different underlying reason: every participant in one meeting needs to be reachable through the same SFU instance so that instance can actually forward media between them, not because of any ordering guarantee.

blocks.alt: Ordinary call volume scales by adding new SFU instances for new meetings; an unusually large webinar instead grows a cascaded, hierarchical layer of leaf SFUs beneath a root

blocks.text: An ordinary meeting comfortably fits on one SFU instance. A ten-thousand-person webinar does not, and forcing it onto a single instance would recreate exactly the kind of single-hot-shard problem discussed in the live comment system's design.

blocks.alt: A presenter's single upload reaches a root SFU, which forwards it to several leaf SFUs, each serving its own batch of viewers, rather than one SFU trying to serve all ten thousand directly

blocks.text: Durable data here is small and low-volume, meeting metadata and participant rosters, so it does not need aggressive sharding the way the comment or message stores in other designs in this category do. Recording storage is the one part that grows meaningfully over time, and it scales the ordinary way object storage scales, sharded by meeting id across a distributed storage system, since recordings are large, immutable blobs with no need for complex querying.

blocks.alt: What actually matters is audio and video staying in sync with each other, which is very noticeable when it drifts; whether every participant agrees on exact data barely matters, since a skipped frame here and there is invisible

blocks.text: Traditional data consistency barely applies to a live media stream in the first place, there is no shared ledger of frames that every participant needs to agree on. What actually matters, and what this design spends real engineering effort protecting, is audio-video synchronization within a single participant's stream, since even a small drift between the sound of someone talking and the movement of their lips is immediately, uncomfortably obvious to a viewer in a way that a dropped frame never is.

blocks.alt: When an SFU instance hosting a call crashes, the signaling server detects it and reassigns the meeting to a new instance, and participants briefly freeze while reconnecting

blocks.text: This is a harder failure to hide gracefully than most of the failovers elsewhere in this document, because unlike a document's content, which can be reconstructed exactly from an operation log, there is no way to replay the last few seconds of a dropped live video stream. The honest goal here is a brief, visible freeze followed by a fast reconnect, not a seamless, invisible recovery.

blocks.alt: Media in transit is always encrypted with SRTP, with keys exchanged over DTLS; joining a meeting requires either the correct password or explicit admission from a waiting room

blocks.text: Beyond encrypting the media itself, meeting access control matters just as much in practice, since an unprotected meeting link being shared or guessed is a far more common real-world security failure than a cryptographic break, which is exactly why waiting rooms and meeting passwords are treated as first-class security features rather than an afterthought.

blocks.text: The metrics that matter most here map directly to what a participant actually experiences: packet loss percentage, jitter, and round-trip time, all measured per participant per call, since these three numbers together are a very good proxy for perceived call quality. A spike in TURN relay usage across many calls at once is also worth watching closely, since it can signal a network provider issue well before enough individual users complain about it.

blocks.text: Bandwidth is the dominant cost in this system, not compute, which flips the usual cost conversation. Minimizing TURN relay usage by improving direct connection success rates saves real money, since every relayed packet is paid for twice, once inbound to the relay and once outbound to its destination. Choosing an SFU over an MCU also saves substantially on compute, since forwarding packets is far cheaper than decoding and re-encoding every stream server-side. Recording storage costs are managed the ordinary way, tiering older recordings to cheaper, colder storage classes over time.

A screen share needs a different quality treatment than camera video, typically higher resolution but a lower frame rate, since shared slides matter more for sharpness than motion smoothness.
A very large webinar's single presenter has their upload become the one thing every viewer depends on, making that one stream's reliability disproportionately important.

blocks.text: Deploying a new SFU version cannot simply restart the process, since that would silently drop every live call it is hosting; a drain approach is needed instead, letting existing calls finish naturally on the old version while new calls land on the updated one. Load testing an SFU deployment needs to simulate realistic packet loss and jitter conditions, not just clean network traffic, since a change that looks fine in a pristine lab network can behave very differently against the messy reality of real-world connections.

blocks.text: End-to-end encryption, where even the SFU cannot see raw media content, is a natural next step for privacy-sensitive use cases, though it is genuinely harder here than in a text messaging system, since the SFU still needs some visibility into simulcast layer structure to make forwarding decisions, typically solved by encrypting the media payload while leaving just enough metadata unencrypted for routing. AI-driven noise suppression and virtual backgrounds are increasingly expected features, most efficiently run on-device rather than adding server-side compute load. Deeper webinar features, like moderated question queues, are a natural extension once the core large-audience broadcast topology from section 17 is solid.

from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, List, Union


# A tiny stand in for a real WebSocket connection, capturing every message
# actually sent to it so this demo can verify delivery.
class WebSocketSession:
    def __init__(self, participant_id: str):
        self._participant_id = participant_id
        self._received: List[object] = []

    def send(self, message: object) -> None:
        self._received.append(message)   # record whatever was sent, whether an SfuAssignment or a SignalingMessage

    def get_received(self) -> List[object]:
        return self._received


# One SDP offer, answer, or ICE candidate being relayed between two clients.
class SignalingMessage:
    def __init__(self, msg_type: str, payload: str):
        self._type = msg_type          # "offer", "answer", or "ice-candidate"
        self._payload = payload           # the actual SDP or candidate content

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"{self._type}: {self._payload}"


# Tells a joining client which SFU instance to connect its media to.
class SfuAssignment:
    def __init__(self, sfu_id: str):
        self._sfu_id = sfu_id

    def get_sfu_id(self) -> str: return self._sfu_id

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"SfuAssignment({self._sfu_id})"


# Relays SDP offers, answers, and ICE candidates between two clients
# setting up a connection to the same SFU. The signaling server never
# touches the actual media, only the handshake messages that precede it.
class SignalingServer:
    def __init__(self):
        self._sessions_by_participant: Dict[str, WebSocketSession] = {}
        self._assigned_sfu_by_meeting: Dict[str, str] = {}

    def on_participant_connect(self, meeting_id: str, participant_id: str, session: WebSocketSession) -> None:
        self._sessions_by_participant[participant_id] = session   # remember this participant's connection
        if meeting_id not in self._assigned_sfu_by_meeting:           # reuse the meeting's SFU if already chosen
            self._assigned_sfu_by_meeting[meeting_id] = self._pick_nearest_healthy_sfu()
        sfu_id = self._assigned_sfu_by_meeting[meeting_id]
        session.send(SfuAssignment(sfu_id))   # tell the client which SFU to connect to

    # Relays an SDP offer or answer, or an ICE candidate, without inspecting its contents.
    def relay_signaling_message(self, from_participant_id: str, to_participant_id: str, message: SignalingMessage) -> None:
        target = self._sessions_by_participant.get(to_participant_id)   # the intended recipient's connection
        if target is not None:
            target.send(message)   # forward it, untouched

    def _pick_nearest_healthy_sfu(self) -> str:
        # In a real system, this consults a service registry and client region.
        return "sfu-instance-1"


class Layer(Enum):
    LOW = "low"
    MEDIUM = "medium"
    HIGH = "high"


# Runs on the SFU: decides, per recipient, which simulcast layer of a
# sender's video to actually forward, based on that recipient's current
# bandwidth estimate.
class SimulcastForwardingDecider:
    # Chooses the highest layer that still fits comfortably within the
    # recipient's estimated available bandwidth, leaving headroom so a
    # small fluctuation does not immediately force another switch.
    def choose_layer_for(self, recipient_bandwidth_kbps: float) -> Layer:
        safety_margin = 0.8                            # only use 80 percent of estimated bandwidth
        usable = recipient_bandwidth_kbps * safety_margin   # the bandwidth this decision actually relies on
        if usable >= 1500:
            return Layer.HIGH        # plenty of headroom, send the best layer
        if usable >= 500:
            return Layer.MEDIUM      # moderate headroom, send the middle layer
        return Layer.LOW             # limited headroom, send the safest layer

    # Called whenever a recipient's bandwidth estimate changes meaningfully,
    # for example after packet loss or jitter measurements shift.
    def reevaluate(self, recipient_id: str, new_bandwidth_kbps: float, current_layer: Layer) -> Layer:
        target = self.choose_layer_for(new_bandwidth_kbps)   # what the new bandwidth estimate calls for
        if target == current_layer:
            return current_layer   # no change needed, avoid unnecessary layer switches
        return target   # switch, the SFU will begin forwarding this layer instead


if __name__ == "__main__":
    signaling_server = SignalingServer()   # the control plane

    alice_session = WebSocketSession("alice")   # alice's signaling connection
    bob_session = WebSocketSession("bob")          # bob's signaling connection

    signaling_server.on_participant_connect("meeting-1", "alice", alice_session)   # alice joins the meeting
    signaling_server.on_participant_connect("meeting-1", "bob", bob_session)          # bob joins the same meeting

    alice_assignment: SfuAssignment = alice_session.get_received()[0]   # what alice was told
    bob_assignment: SfuAssignment = bob_session.get_received()[0]          # what bob was told
    print(f"Alice assigned to: {alice_assignment.get_sfu_id()}")
    print(f"Bob assigned to: {bob_assignment.get_sfu_id()}")
    print(f"Both participants share the same SFU: {str(alice_assignment.get_sfu_id() == bob_assignment.get_sfu_id()).lower()}")

    # Alice sends an SDP offer to Bob, relayed untouched by the signaling server.
    signaling_server.relay_signaling_message("alice", "bob", SignalingMessage("offer", "v=0 o=alice ..."))
    print(f"Messages Bob received: {len(bob_session.get_received())}")   # the SFU assignment, plus the relayed offer
    print(f"Bob's latest message: {bob_session.get_received()[-1]}")

    # Now demonstrate the SFU's simulcast layer decisions for a few different bandwidth estimates.
    decider = SimulcastForwardingDecider()
    print(f"Layer for 2000 kbps: {decider.choose_layer_for(2000).name}")  # plenty of bandwidth
    print(f"Layer for 700 kbps: {decider.choose_layer_for(700).name}")      # moderate bandwidth
    print(f"Layer for 200 kbps: {decider.choose_layer_for(200).name}")        # weak bandwidth

    stable_layer = decider.reevaluate("carol", 2100, Layer.HIGH)
    print(f"Reevaluating a stable, still-strong connection stays at: {stable_layer.name}")

    downgraded_layer = decider.reevaluate("carol", 300, Layer.HIGH)
    print(f"Reevaluating after bandwidth drops downgrades to: {downgraded_layer.name}")

items: Architecture: a signaling path and a media path that almost never intersect, an SFU that forwards rather than transcodes, and a TURN relay fallback for restrictive networks.
Capacity: a million concurrent calls at peak, typical calls of four to six participants, webinars reaching up to ten thousand viewers, and roughly 1.5 megabits per second per HD participant.
The core trade-off: mesh versus SFU versus MCU, compared directly on client upload cost, server compute cost, and where each one breaks down.
Database: a deliberately thin schema, since almost all live-call state is ephemeral and lives only in the SFU's memory for the duration of a call.
End-to-end workflows: the call join handshake and adaptive simulcast downgrade under degrading bandwidth, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: what matters is audio-video sync within one stream, not agreement across participants on exact data, a genuinely different notion of correctness than every other system in this category.
Production considerations: connection-draining SFU deployments and load testing against realistic packet loss and jitter, not clean lab conditions.
